title: Labelling الْمُبْتَدَأ and الْخَبَر, Classifying Sentences, and Breaking Each Word into اسْم، فِعْل، حَرْف
summary: The class applies the grammar it has just learned to read in Arabic. Students pick out the مُبْتَدَأ and الْخَبَر in sentence after sentence, then classify sentences as اسْمِيَّة or فِعْلِيَّة — discovering that الْمُدَرِّسُ خَرَجَ is nominal even though it contains a verb, because what matters is the first word. They then break whole sentences down word by word into اسْم، فِعْل and حَرْف, which turns up some surprises: بَعْدَ is a noun, هُوَ is a noun, and مَا can be either depending on its use.
key_points: Identifying the parts of a nominal sentence: in الْمَاءُ قَلِيلٌ the مُبْتَدَأ is الْمَاء and the خَبَر is قَلِيل; likewise سُعَادُ مُمَرِّضَةٌ، الْقَهْوَةُ بَارِدَةٌ، النُّجُومُ جَمِيلَةٌ، الدُّخُولُ مَمْنُوعٌ، الْبَابُ مُغْلَقٌ.

What makes a sentence فِعْلِيَّة is that it begins with a verb, not that it contains one. خَرَجَ الْمُدَرِّسُ is فِعْلِيَّة, but الْمُدَرِّسُ خَرَجَ is اسْمِيَّة — the same two words in the other order.

Breaking a sentence into the three categories throws up cases that look deceptive: بَعْدَ is an اسْم, not a حَرْف; هُوَ is an اسْم, being a pronoun; and أل is counted as part of the word it attaches to rather than separately.
مَا can be either an اسْم or a حَرْف depending on its use: as الْمَوْصُولَة it is a noun, but where it negates it is a حَرْف.
لَمْ and لَمَّا leave نُون النِّسْوَة untouched — لَمْ يَكْتُبْنَ — while تَذْهَبِينَ loses its نُون to give لَمْ تَذْهَبِي, and a singular verb simply takes the sukūn.
اللَّائِي is the same as اللَّاتِي, the plural feminine relative pronoun, written with a hamza in place of the tāʾ.

Lesson 22 could be skipped because it only reviews the verb's three states, which the class already knows: مَرْفُوع as the default with a ḍamma, مَنْصُوب with a fatḥa or a dropped نُون, and مَجْزُوم with a sukūn or a dropped نُون.
أَبُو becomes أَبِي when it falls in a genitive position — أَبِي الْحَسَنِ means the father of al-Ḥasan, not my father. The form is easily mistaken for the أَبِي that carries the possessive yāʾ.

Numbers continue to be drilled in context: خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا with its singular counted noun in the accusative, and ثَلَاثٌ وَخَمْسُونَ صَفْحَةً with the number's gender reversed against صَفْحَة.
الْآخَرُونَ is جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم, showing its case with a wāw.

Vocabulary: مُمَرِّضَة (nurse), بَارِد (cold), مَمْنُوع (forbidden, as in الدُّخُولُ مَمْنُوعٌ), مُغْلَق (closed), ذَكِيّ (clever), زَهْرَة (a flower, also used as a name), كَنَسَ (to sweep), فَاكِهَة (fruit), وَزِير (minister), and الشَّيْخ الْكَرِيم (the honoured shaykh).

The lesson's dialogue previews قِصَص الْأَنْبِيَاء, the Stories of the Prophets — the Arabic reader the teacher had earlier suggested taking up after this book, since it applies the grammar to a real text.
questions: [00:06:06] Q: What does لَمْ do to the verb after it? — A: It makes it sākin; where the verb carries a نُون, that نُون is dropped instead — except نُون النِّسْوَة, which does not change.
[00:08:13] Q: When do you use يَأْكُلُ rather than تَأْكُلُ? — A: يَأْكُلُ is the third person, for speaking about someone; تَأْكُلُ is for addressing the person directly.
[00:11:00] Q: Why يَرْجِعُ rather than يَخْرُجُ there? — A: Either works — the minister did not leave London, or he did not return from London. Both fit the sentence.
[00:15:00] Q: Is الْمُدَرِّسُ خَرَجَ not a جُمْلَة فِعْلِيَّة, since it has a verb in it? — A: No. What decides it is the first word, and this one begins with an اسْم, so it is اسْمِيَّة.
[00:16:00] Q: Is اللَّهُ a verb in that sentence? — A: No, it is an اسْم, so the sentence is اسْمِيَّة.
[00:18:00] Q: Isn't بَعْدَ a حَرْف? — A: No, بَعْدَ is an اسْم.
[00:20:03] Q: Is the أل of الْأَحْمَر counted as a separate word? — A: No, treat it as part of the same word.
[00:22:06] Q: Is هُوَ a حَرْف? — A: No, it is an اسْم — a pronoun is a noun.
[00:23:00] Q: Can مَا be an اسْم? — A: Yes, it can; but in this sentence it is negating, so here it is a حَرْف.
[00:30:02] Q: Why is there a yāʾ in أَبِي — is he talking about his own father? — A: No. أَبُو becomes أَبِي in a genitive position, so أَبِي الْحَسَنِ is the father of al-Ḥasan.
[00:23:00] Q: What is اللَّائِي? — A: The same as اللَّاتِي, the plural feminine relative pronoun, spelled with a hamza instead of a tāʾ.

quiz.q: In الْمَاءُ قَلِيلٌ, which word is the خَبَر?
quiz.a: الْمَاء is the subject being spoken about and قَلِيل is the information given about it.

quiz.q: Is الْمُدَرِّسُ خَرَجَ nominal or verbal?
options: Verbal, because it contains a verb
Nominal, because its first word is a noun
quiz.a: The classification depends on the opening word alone — the same two words as خَرَجَ الْمُدَرِّسُ, but in the other order.

quiz.q: What category does بَعْدَ belong to?
quiz.a: A point that surprised the class: despite looking like a particle, بَعْدَ is a noun.

quiz.q: What category does هُوَ belong to?
Can مَا be both an اسْم and a حَرْف?
options: No, it is always a حَرْف
Yes — as الْمَوْصُولَة it is an اسْم, but when negating it is a حَرْف
No, it is always an اسْم
quiz.a: Its category follows its use, which is why the three types of مَا had to be distinguished earlier.

quiz.q: What does لَمْ do to يَكْتُبْنَ?
options: Nothing — نُون النِّسْوَة does not change
quiz.a: لَمْ يَكْتُبْنَ stays as it is, while تَذْهَبِينَ would become لَمْ تَذْهَبِي.
The same plural feminine relative pronoun, written with a hamza in place of the tāʾ.

quiz.q: What does أَبِي mean in أَبِي الْحَسَنِ?
options: The father of al-Ḥasan — أَبُو in a genitive position
quiz.a: The yāʾ here is the genitive form of أَبُو, not the possessive yāʾ — a confusion the teacher had to clear up.

quiz.q: What are the three states of the verb that Lesson 22 reviews?
quiz.a: The default with a ḍamma, the accusative with a fatḥa or dropped نُون, and the jussive with a sukūn or dropped نُون.

quiz.q: What does الدُّخُولُ مَمْنُوعٌ mean, and what is the مُبْتَدَأ?
options: Entry is forbidden — مَمْنُوع is the مُبْتَدَأ
Entry is forbidden — الدُّخُول is the مُبْتَدَأ
Exit is forbidden — الدُّخُول is the خَبَر
No entry — there is no مُبْتَدَأ
quiz.a: الدُّخُول, itself a مَصْدَر, is the subject, and مَمْنُوع the information given about it.

quran_examples.arabic: اللَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ
quran_examples.transliteration: allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa al-ḥayyu al-qayyūm
quran_examples.translation: Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence.
quran_examples.note: A جُمْلَة اسْمِيَّة of the kind the class was labelling: it opens with an اسْم, and هُوَ within it is itself an اسْم, being a pronoun.

quran_examples.translation: When the victory of Allah has come, and the conquest.
quran_examples.note: A جُمْلَة فِعْلِيَّة: جَاءَ is the verb and نَصْرُ اللَّهِ its فَاعِل, carrying the ḍamma — the structure the exercise asked students to recognise.

quran_examples.translation: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
quran_examples.note: Nominal in form, with الْحَمْد as the مُبْتَدَأ; the لَام is a حَرْف and الْعَالَمِينَ a جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم showing its case by letter.

quran_examples.arabic: وَاللَّائِي يَئِسْنَ مِنَ الْمَحِيضِ مِن نِّسَائِكُمْ
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-llāʾī yaʾisna mina al-maḥīḍi min nisāʾikum
quran_examples.translation: And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation…
quran_examples.note: The Qur'ānic form of اللَّائِي the teacher mentioned as equivalent to اللَّاتِي; يَئِسْنَ beside it carries نُون النِّسْوَة.
